title: How to Drink a Tree's Blood
summary: Josh and Chuck (transcript labels one host as iHeart Intro) explore maple syrup: the sugar maple tree and its sap, the tapping window in late winter, Indigenous North American sugaring methods and sugar making, colonial-era spread and the abolitionist sugar boycott angle, industrialization (vacuum tubing, reverse osmosis, propane), climate threats and Vermont's biodiversity rule, the Jones rule of 86 and tree health, boiling and processing, terroir, Quebec's PPAQ producer group and the 2011-2012 maple syrup heist, global production including South Korea goro tree sap and Pacific Northwest big leaf maple, grading (Grade A colors, processing grade), storage and mold, maple candy and other maple products, nutrition, and a listener mail note about kerosene as jet fuel.

segments.title: Opening banter and maple cravings
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the maple syrup topic, suggested by listener Olivia, and joke about wanting maple. They mention the title and a possible parenthetical.

segments.title: Sugar maple trees and where they grow
segments.summary: Sugar maples have the highest sap sugar concentration and are the preferred source. Their range covers northeastern US, southeastern Canada, and parts of Ontario and Maine down to North Carolina. Southern Quebec is the largest producer. Climate conditions make production resistant to industrialization.

segments.title: Sap, xylem, and the sugaring window
segments.summary: Sap is the xylem fluid that moves water, minerals and hormones through the tree. Tapping works best February to April, peaking in March, when freezing nights and thawing days build pressure and starches stored as sugars make the sap sweetest.

segments.title: Sap sugar content and boiling down
segments.summary: Sap runs about one to three percent sugar, so it must be boiled to about sixty-six percent sugar. Roughly forty gallons of sap yield one gallon of syrup.
topics: forty gallons per gallon of syrup

segments.title: Jones rule of 86 and origin stories
segments.summary: C. W. Jones's rule of 86 estimates gallons of sap needed per gallon of syrup from sugar percentage. Hosts discuss legends of how Indigenous people first discovered sap, such as a tomahawk in a tree, a woodpecker hole, or a sapsicle.

segments.title: Indigenous tapping methods and sugar making
segments.summary: Indigenous groups including the Abenaki, Mohican, Ojibwa and Algonquin tapped sugar maples by cutting bark, using twig taps, and collecting sap in birch bark containers. They boiled sap with heated rocks, over fire, or in the sun, and used freezing to remove water. They also made maple sugar cakes.

segments.title: Seasonal life and sugaring vocabulary
segments.summary: Ojibwa communities gathered in spring after winter dispersal, with sugaring season as a key start to that gathering. Hosts explain the terms sugaring season, sugar shack, and sugar bush.

segments.title: Home sugaring and sugar shacks
segments.summary: Hosts discuss small-scale home sugaring, including evaporation pans sold by supply houses, steam concerns indoors, and the appeal of a backyard sugar shack.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break and transition back from the break.

segments.title: Metal pots, colonial sugaring, and abolitionists
segments.summary: European colonists adopted local sugaring methods and metal pots improved processing. Maple sugar was cheaper than Caribbean cane sugar. Abolitionists and Quakers, including Benjamin Rush, promoted maple as an alternative to slave-produced sugar. Thomas Jefferson supported the idea as a farm economy.

segments.title: Decline of maple sugar and pancake syrup
segments.summary: Maple production stayed labor-intensive and fell as cane and beet sugar became cheaper in the late nineteenth century. Producers blended maple with cane sugar and corn syrup, leading to brands like Mrs. Butterworth's.

segments.title: Real versus table syrup and storage
segments.summary: Hosts compare real maple syrup with pancake syrup and childhood imitation maple syrup. Josh learned real syrup must be refrigerated after opening, unlike pancake syrup. Chuck mentions mold concerns in his pantry syrup.
topics: real maple syrup vs pancake syrup

segments.title: Vacuum tubing, reverse osmosis, and industrialization
segments.summary: From the 1970s, vacuum pumps and plastic tubing replaced buckets. Reverse osmosis removes about ninety percent of water before boiling, and propane replaced wood fires. Production rose about four hundred percent by the mid-1990s in the US and Canada. Greens Sugar House still uses wood.

segments.title: Climate change, sugar maple range, and biodiversity
segments.summary: Warmer temperatures, less snow cover, disease, and invasive species threaten sugar maples and may shrink their range northward. Monoculture sugar bushes reduce biodiversity, and Vermont requires at least twenty-five percent of trees in a sugar bush to be other species.

segments.title: Tree age, size, and whether tapping harms trees
segments.summary: Trees must be about forty years old and at least ten inches in diameter, generally tapped once, and sometimes twice if over eighteen inches. C. W. Jones (called Doctor Jones) at University of Vermont estimated tapping removes four to nine percent of carbohydrate reserves, so harm is limited.

segments.title: Commercial processing and turkey fryer story
segments.summary: Small producers boil in sugar houses; larger operations collect sap to central boil locations. Chuck's turkey fryer repurposing is mentioned, along with a warning against frying turkeys indoors.

segments.title: Maple flavor and the Maillard reaction
segments.summary: Maple flavor forms mostly during heating through the Maillard reaction and caramelization rather than being present in sap. The hosts refer to their toast episode.

segments.title: Filtering sugar sand and terroir
segments.summary: After boiling, sugar sand must be filtered out. Hosts compare maple terroir to wine terroir, where a specialized producer's tree and soil can command higher prices.

segments.title: Quebec's PPAQ and the maple syrup cartel
segments.summary: Quebec produces about seventy-two percent of the world's maple syrup with about fifty-five million taps and about eight thousand producers. The government-endorsed PPAQ acts as intermediary, sets marketing and pricing, holds a strategic reserve started in 2000, and takes a cut from all producers. Critics call it a cartel or mafia.

segments.title: Canada trade and US top producers
segments.summary: Canada is the largest exporter of maple syrup, with about 457 million dollars of sales in 2023 cited, and the US imports more than it exports. Vermont, New York, and other states are the top US producers.

segments.title: Maple syrup heist of 2011 to 2012
segments.summary: Thieves siphoned about 2,700 tons of syrup from barrels in a PPAQ strategic reserve warehouse starting in 2011, filling them with water or leaving them empty. An audit revealed it. About 450 tons were recovered, and Richard Valliers was sentenced to seven years and ten months.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break and return to the show.

segments.title: Other maple sap around the world
segments.summary: Birch and other maple sap are used for beer, vinegar, and drinks. South Korea's goro maple sap is drunk in saunas as a health tonic. Northern China drinks maple sap, and Pacific Northwest big leaf maples are tapped but need about twice as much sap per gallon of syrup.

segments.title: Maple syrup grading and processing grade
segments.summary: Syrup grades were once Fancy, A, and B, changed to all Grade A with color and flavor categories: golden (delicate), amber (rich), dark (robust), and very dark (strong). Lower-quality syrup goes to processing grade for industrial foods like Waffle Crisp cereal.

segments.title: Shelf life and other maple products
segments.summary: Unopened syrup keeps about three years on the shelf and then can be refrigerated for another three years. Maple candies, maple cream, and sugar on snow are described as alternatives.

segments.title: Maple foods, sugar, and nutrition
segments.summary: Hosts mention maple cream, maple pie, and maple cotton candy, and that maple sugar can replace granulated sugar in baking. They discuss nutrition: high manganese, riboflavin, potassium, calcium, zinc, antioxidants, and a lower glycemic index than sugar. Some compounds may enhance antibiotics.

segments.title: Listener mail: kerosene as jet fuel
segments.summary: Listener Kyle Metzker writes that kerosene has been jet fuel nearly always, correcting the host's surprise about the Concorde's fuel from an older episode, noting kerosene's uses in jet fuel and household cooking and lighting.

segments.summary: Closing credits and promotion for iHeartRadio podcasts.
